==================================================
24. PHASE 12 COMPLETION CRITERIA
==================================================

Phase 12 is complete when:

1. The Phase-10 encoder checkpoint loads successfully.

2. The Phase-11 generative decoder checkpoint loads successfully.

3. Phase-10 latent vectors are verified.

4. Baseline latent dimension remains 32.

5. Predictor label space is derived from training data only.

6. Baseline biological-relevance predictor is implemented.

7. Predictor is trained using training molecules only.

8. Validation data is used for predictor model selection.

9. Test data is excluded from predictor model selection.

10. Best predictor checkpoint is saved.

11. Best predictor checkpoint reloads successfully.

12. Encoder parameters are frozen.

13. Decoder parameters are frozen.

14. Predictor parameters are frozen after training.

15. θE* is preserved.

16. θD* is preserved.

17. θP* is established.

18. Z0 is saved.

19. All baseline latent vectors are finite.

20. Phase-8 split assignments remain unchanged.

21. Fisher reference subset remains unchanged.

22. Model hashes are saved.

23. Θ* metadata is saved.

24. No closed-loop adaptation has occurred.

25. No EWC has occurred.

26. No parameter drift has yet been introduced.

27. The baseline system is ready to serve as the reference state for later
    continual adaptation.


==================================================
IMPORTANT TERMINOLOGY AFTER PHASE 12
==================================================

After successful Phase 12 it is appropriate to state:

"The complete baseline molecular discovery system was consolidated and frozen
as the reference state Θ*."


It is also appropriate to state:

"The baseline parameter state comprises the trained encoder, molecular
generative decoder, and DrugBank-grounded biological-relevance predictor."


And:

"The baseline latent molecular representation Z0 was retained as the reference
latent state for subsequent drift analysis."


Do NOT yet claim:

"The system has self-evolved."

"The model has improved through feedback."

"The model has performed continual learning."

"Parameter drift has occurred."

"EWC has preserved prior knowledge."


Those statements only become valid after later adaptive-learning stages.


==================================================
FINAL PHASE 12 WORKFLOW
==================================================

DrugBank-Derived Baseline Corpus
        ↓
Phase-10 Trained Encoder
        ↓
θE*
        ↓
Baseline Latent Representation Z0
        ↓
Phase-11 Trained Molecular Decoder
        ↓
θD*
        ↓
DrugBank Biological Associations
        ↓
Training-Only Predictor Label Space
        ↓
Baseline Predictor Training
        ↓
θP*
        ↓
        ┌───────────────────────┐
        │         Θ*            │
        │                       │
        │  θE*                  │
        │  θD*                  │
        │  θP*                  │
        └───────────────────────┘
                  ↓
      Baseline Reference Snapshot
                  ↓
      Model Hash / Integrity Record
                  ↓
      Reference State for Later Drift,
      Fisher Information, EWC and
      Closed-Loop Adaptation


NEXT PHASE

Phase 13 — Fisher Information Estimation and Continual-Learning Reference
Construction



---
========================

# PHASE 13 — BASELINE KNOWLEDGE CONSOLIDATION AND FISHER INFORMATION REFERENCE CONSTRUCTION


## OBJECTIVE

Phase 13 is performed after establishment of the frozen baseline model state in Phase 12 and before the first closed-loop adaptation cycle.

Phase 12 established the complete baseline parameter state:

\[
\Theta^*
=
\{
\theta_E^*,
\theta_D^*,
\theta_P^*
\}
\]

where:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

represents the trained baseline geometry-aware molecular encoder,

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

represents the trained latent-conditioned molecular generative decoder,

and:

\[
\theta_P^*
\]

represents the trained DrugBank-grounded target-association predictor.

Phase 12 also established the fixed deterministic baseline latent representation:

\[
Z_0
\]

Phase 13 does not retrain these components.

Instead, Phase 13 estimates how important individual baseline model parameters are for preserving the previously learned DrugBank-grounded target-association task.

The primary mechanism used for this purpose is a:

**DIAGONAL EMPIRICAL FISHER INFORMATION APPROXIMATION**

The resulting parameter-importance values will later be used by Elastic Weight Consolidation, or EWC, during continual adaptation.

Conceptually:

```text
Frozen Baseline System Θ*
        ↓
Fixed Training-Derived Fisher Reference Corpus
        ↓
Baseline Target-Association Objective
        ↓
Parameter Gradients
        ↓
Square Per-Sample Gradients
        ↓
Average Across Fisher Reference Molecules
        ↓
Diagonal Fisher Importance
        ↓
F_E + F_P
        ↓
Consolidated Baseline Knowledge State K0
```


==================================================
## IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
==================================================

Phase 13 estimates parameter importance.

It does **not** modify the baseline model.

Phase 13 performs:

```text
Fisher-gradient calculation
parameter-importance estimation
reference-state consolidation
integrity verification
```

Phase 13 does **not** perform:

```text
optimizer updates
parameter optimization
EWC regularization
continual learning
candidate optimization
closed-loop feedback
UCB acquisition
decoder adaptation
encoder adaptation
predictor adaptation
```

Therefore:

\[
\Theta_{\text{after Phase 13}}
=
\Theta^*
\]

The baseline parameters must remain exactly unchanged.


==================================================
## 1. INPUT BASELINE STATE
==================================================

Phase 13 begins from the finalized Phase-12 baseline state:

\[
\Theta^*
=
\{
\theta_E^*,
\theta_D^*,
\theta_P^*
\}
\]

with:

### Encoder

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

Trained geometry-aware variational molecular encoder from Phase 10.

Its deterministic molecular representation is:

\[
z=\mu
\]


### Generative Decoder

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

Trained strongly latent-conditioned molecular generative decoder from Phase 11.


### Biological-Relevance Predictor

\[
\theta_P^*
\]

Trained DrugBank-grounded multi-label target-association predictor from Phase 12.


### Latent Reference

\[
Z_0
\]

Fixed deterministic baseline latent molecular representation established in Phase 10 and consolidated in Phase 12.


Additional Phase-12 information reused in Phase 13 includes:

```text
training-only predictor latent normalization
training-only target vocabulary
training-derived positive class weights
baseline parameter hashes
Θ* reference bundle
```

Phase-9/10 graph-feature normalization is also reused without modification.


==================================================
## 2. FISHER REFERENCE CORPUS
==================================================

The Fisher calculation uses the fixed Phase-8 Fisher-reference subset.

Current Fisher reference size:

\[
N=128
\]

molecules.

These molecules were selected exclusively from the training corpus.

Therefore:

\[
D_{\text{Fisher}}
\subset
D_{\text{train}}
\]

and:

\[
D_{\text{Fisher}}
\cap
D_{\text{validation}}
=
\varnothing
\]

\[
D_{\text{Fisher}}
\cap
D_{\text{test}}
=
\varnothing
\]

The Fisher-reference subset is fixed.

It must not be regenerated, resampled, or replaced during Phase 13 or future comparison cycles.

This ensures that future importance calculations remain comparable.


==================================================
## 3. WHY A DIAGONAL FISHER APPROXIMATION IS USED
==================================================

A complete Fisher information matrix would contain covariance relationships among every pair of model parameters.

For a model containing tens of thousands of parameters, the full matrix would be computationally expensive and unnecessary for the intended EWC implementation.

Therefore Phase 13 uses a diagonal approximation.

For every model parameter element:

\[
\theta_j
\]

a single importance value is retained:

\[
F_j
\]

Thus:

```text
parameter θ1 → F1
parameter θ2 → F2
parameter θ3 → F3
...
```

Only the diagonal parameter importance values are stored.

This provides a computationally practical importance estimate suitable for later EWC regularization.


==================================================
## 4. EMPIRICAL FISHER DEFINITION
==================================================

For Fisher-reference molecule \(i\) and model parameter \(\theta_j\):

\[
g_{ij}
=
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}
{\partial \theta_j}
\]

where:

\[
\mathcal{L}_i
\]

is the baseline task loss for Fisher-reference molecule \(i\).

The diagonal empirical Fisher approximation is:

\[
F_j
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
g_{ij}^{2}
\]

or equivalently:

\[
F_j
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left(
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}
{\partial \theta_j}
\right)^2
\]

where:

\[
N=128
\]

for the current Fisher-reference corpus.

A relatively large:

\[
F_j
\]

means the baseline task loss is more sensitive to changes in that parameter under the defined Fisher objective and reference dataset.

A relatively small:

\[
F_j
\]

means the parameter is less strongly constrained by this particular baseline objective.

Fisher importance therefore represents:

**model-parameter importance under the defined task**

and not universal chemical or biological importance.


==================================================
## 5. FISHER INFORMATION REQUIRES A DEFINED TASK
==================================================

Fisher importance is meaningful only with respect to a specified model objective.

It is not appropriate to calculate arbitrary gradients and describe them as generic knowledge importance.

For the current system, the baseline biological objective is:

**DrugBank-grounded multi-label target-association prediction**

Therefore the Phase-13 Fisher calculation is based on the frozen Phase-12 predictor objective.


==================================================
## 6. PRIMARY FISHER OBJECTIVE
==================================================

The primary Fisher loss is:

**multi-label target-association Binary Cross Entropy with Logits**

Conceptually:

```text
Fisher-reference molecular graph
        ↓
Baseline Encoder θE*
        ↓
Deterministic latent μ
        ↓
Frozen Phase-12 latent normalization
        ↓
Baseline Predictor θP*
        ↓
130 target-association logits
        ↓
DrugBank-derived target-association labels
        ↓
BCEWithLogitsLoss
        ↓
Backpropagation
        ↓
Per-sample gradients
        ↓
Squared gradients
        ↓
Fisher accumulation
```


The baseline Fisher objective therefore preserves knowledge associated with:

```text
learned molecular representation
+
DrugBank-grounded target-association prediction
```


==================================================
## 7. PARAMETERS INCLUDED IN FISHER ESTIMATION
==================================================

The primary Fisher parameter set is:

\[
\theta_E^*
+
\theta_P^*
\]

Therefore Phase 13 calculates:

\[
F_E
\]

for encoder parameters,

and:

\[
F_P
\]

for predictor parameters.


This design is appropriate because future EWC-controlled adaptation may modify:

```text
encoder parameters
and/or
predictor parameters
```


==================================================
## 8. DECODER POLICY
==================================================

The generative decoder:

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

does not directly participate in the DrugBank target-association prediction loss.

Therefore predictor BCE gradients do not provide a meaningful Fisher estimate for decoder parameters.

Consequently:

\[
F_D
\]

is **not calculated** in the current baseline Phase 13 implementation.

Instead:

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

is preserved as a frozen baseline checkpoint.

If a future methodology explicitly allows decoder adaptation, decoder-specific importance should be estimated separately using a generation-specific objective such as SELFIES next-token negative log-likelihood.


==================================================
## 9. OPTIONAL FUTURE DECODER FISHER
==================================================

If future adaptation modifies the decoder, a separate decoder Fisher could be estimated using:

```text
reference latent representation
        ↓
baseline decoder θD*
        ↓
SELFIES token probability distribution
        ↓
reference SELFIES sequence
        ↓
token-level cross-entropy
        ↓
decoder gradients
        ↓
squared gradients
        ↓
F_D
```

In such a future extension:

\[
F
=
\{
F_E,
F_D,
F_P
\}
\]

However, the current baseline implementation deliberately uses:

\[
F
=
\{
F_E,
F_P
\}
\]


==================================================
## 10. ACTUAL ENCODER COMPUTATIONAL GRAPH
==================================================

Phase 12 predictor training used saved deterministic Phase-10 latent vectors.

That was appropriate because Phase 12 trained only:

\[
\theta_P
\]

and deliberately preserved:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

However, stored latent vectors cannot be used to estimate encoder Fisher.

To calculate:

\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}
{\partial \theta_E}
\]

the actual encoder computational graph must remain connected.

Therefore Phase 13 uses:

```text
Phase-7 molecular graph
        ↓
actual Phase-10 encoder architecture
        ↓
θE* checkpoint
        ↓
deterministic μ
        ↓
predictor
        ↓
loss
```

The final implementation searches the active notebook environment for the previously instantiated Phase-10 encoder architecture whose state-dictionary structure matches the Phase-10 checkpoint.

That encoder architecture is copied and loaded with:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

This ensures that the Fisher calculation uses the same trained encoder computational structure rather than a reconstructed approximation.


==================================================
## 11. DETERMINISTIC LATENT REPRESENTATION
==================================================

The Fisher calculation uses:

\[
z=\mu
\]

rather than stochastic variational sampling.

Therefore:

```text
graph
↓
encoder
↓
μ
↓
predictor
```

is used.

The stochastic representation:

\[
z
=
\mu
+
\sigma\epsilon
\]

is not used for Fisher estimation.

This avoids unnecessary sampling noise and produces a reproducible importance reference.


==================================================
## 12. GRAPH-FEATURE NORMALIZATION
==================================================

The molecular encoder receives graph node features using the same normalization established during Phase 9 and reused during Phase 10.

No new feature normalization is fitted during Phase 13.

Therefore:

```text
Phase-9/10 training-derived normalization
        ↓
reused unchanged in Phase 13
```

The normalization statistics remain part of the frozen preprocessing state.


==================================================
## 13. PHASE-12 LATENT NORMALIZATION
==================================================

The deterministic encoder output:

\[
\mu
\]

is passed to the predictor using the same training-only latent normalization established in Phase 12.

For latent dimension \(k\):

\[
z'_k
=
\frac{
z_k-\mu_{\text{train},k}
}{
\sigma_{\text{train},k}
}
\]

These statistics remain fixed.

They are not recomputed using the Fisher subset.


==================================================
## 14. TARGET VOCABULARY
==================================================

Phase 13 reuses the exact frozen Phase-12 target vocabulary.

Current number of predictor target classes:

\[
K=130
\]

The following operations are prohibited during Phase 13:

```text
recalculating target support
adding new targets
removing target classes
reordering target classes
rebuilding the target vocabulary
```

The Fisher task must remain identical to the Phase-12 predictor task.


==================================================
## 15. TARGET LABEL CONSTRUCTION
==================================================

For each Fisher-reference molecule:

\[
y_i
\in
\{0,1\}^{130}
\]

A target position is:

\[
1
\]

when the corresponding DrugBank target association is present,

and:

\[
0
\]

otherwise.

Duplicate DrugBank rows corresponding to the same:

```text
drug_id + target_id
```

are collapsed into a single binary association.

Therefore the predictor models association presence rather than XML row multiplicity.


==================================================
## 16. CLASS-WEIGHT CONSISTENCY
==================================================

Phase 13 reuses the exact positive class weights established during Phase 12.

These weights were calculated from training data only.

Phase 13 does not calculate new class weights from the 128 Fisher-reference molecules.

Doing so would redefine the baseline predictor task.

The Fisher loss therefore remains consistent with the finalized Phase-12 objective.


==================================================
## 17. SAMPLE-WISE FISHER ESTIMATION
==================================================

The Fisher reference is processed one molecule at a time.

Thus:

\[
B=1
\]

For each Fisher-reference molecule:

1. Zero encoder and predictor gradients.

2. Load the saved molecular graph.

3. Apply the frozen Phase-9/10 graph-feature normalization.

4. Pass the graph through the actual baseline encoder:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

5. Extract deterministic:

\[
\mu
\]

6. Apply the frozen Phase-12 latent normalization.

7. Pass the normalized latent representation through:

\[
\theta_P^*
\]

8. Construct the 130-dimensional DrugBank target-association vector.

9. Compute:

\[
\mathcal{L}_i
=
\operatorname{BCEWithLogitsLoss}
\]

10. Backpropagate the sample loss.

11. Read the gradient for each included parameter.

12. Square the gradient immediately:

\[
g_{ij}^2
\]

13. Add the squared gradient to the Fisher accumulator.

No optimizer update occurs.

After all 128 molecules:

\[
F_j
=
\frac{F_j}{128}
\]


==================================================
## 18. CRITICAL MATHEMATICAL DISTINCTION
==================================================

The correct empirical Fisher calculation is:

\[
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_i
g_i^2
\]

The following shortcut would be incorrect:

\[
\left(
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_i
g_i
\right)^2
\]

because:

**average squared gradient**

is not equal to:

**square of average gradient**

The implementation therefore uses:

```text
individual sample gradient
↓
square gradient
↓
accumulate
↓
average after all molecules
```


==================================================
## 19. NO PARAMETER UPDATES
==================================================

An optimizer is not required for Fisher estimation.

Therefore Phase 13 does not instantiate an optimizer.

The computational sequence is:

```text
zero gradients
↓
forward pass
↓
loss calculation
↓
backward pass
↓
read gradient
↓
square gradient
↓
accumulate Fisher
↓
next molecule
```

The following operation never occurs:

```text
optimizer.step()
```

Thus Fisher estimation does not modify the baseline parameters.


==================================================
## 20. MODEL MODE DURING FISHER ESTIMATION
==================================================

The encoder and predictor operate in deterministic evaluation-compatible mode.

The Phase-12 predictor contains dropout.

Therefore the predictor is placed in:

```text
eval()
```

mode.

This prevents random dropout masks from changing the Fisher reference.

Evaluation mode does not disable gradient calculation.

Gradients are still calculated because parameter gradients remain enabled during the Fisher computation.


==================================================
## 21. PARAMETER STORAGE
==================================================

For every Fisher-controlled parameter, Phase 13 preserves:

```text
parameter name
tensor shape
number of parameter elements
baseline parameter value θ*
Fisher tensor F
```

Encoder parameter names include structures such as:

```text
node_embedding
egnn_layers
graph_mlp
mu_head
```

Predictor parameter names include:

```text
predictor.network
```

The baseline parameter values are preserved alongside their Fisher tensors so they can later be used directly in the EWC penalty.


==================================================
## 22. INACTIVE PARAMETER POLICY
==================================================

Not every encoder parameter is guaranteed to receive a gradient under the deterministic target-association Fisher objective.

If:

```text
parameter.grad is None
```

the parameter is treated as inactive under the current Fisher pathway.

Its accumulated Fisher remains:

\[
F_j=0
\]

This is not considered a computational failure.


==================================================
## 23. LOGVAR POLICY
==================================================

Because Phase 13 uses:

\[
z=\mu
\]

the variational:

```text
logvar_head
```

is excluded from the deterministic predictor pathway.

Therefore its parameters may receive no gradient.

This is expected.

The final implementation does not artificially assign Fisher importance to the log-variance branch.


==================================================
## 24. OTHER INACTIVE BRANCHES
==================================================

Parameters other than the log-variance branch may also receive no gradient under this specific downstream objective.

In the observed Phase-13 calculation, six encoder parameter tensors were inactive:

```text
egnn_layers.1.coordinate_mlp.0.bias
egnn_layers.1.coordinate_mlp.0.weight
egnn_layers.1.coordinate_mlp.2.bias
egnn_layers.1.coordinate_mlp.2.weight
logvar_head.bias
logvar_head.weight
```

No predictor parameter tensor was inactive.

This does **not** mean these encoder parameters are globally unimportant.

It means that under the specific:

```text
deterministic μ
+
DrugBank target-association BCE
+
128-molecule Fisher reference
```

pathway, they did not receive a gradient.

Therefore:

\[
F_j=0
\]

should be interpreted as:

**inactive or unconstrained under this Fisher objective**

and not:

**universally irrelevant parameter**.


==================================================
## 25. FISHER NON-NEGATIVITY
==================================================

Because Fisher is calculated from squared gradients:

\[
F_j \ge 0
\]

for all parameter elements.

Phase 13 validates that Fisher tensors contain:

```text
no negative values
no NaN values
no positive infinity
no negative infinity
```

Any violation would invalidate the Fisher reference.


==================================================
## 26. FISHER SPARSITY
==================================================

Some Fisher elements may equal:

\[
0
\]

Possible explanations include:

```text
inactive computation branch
deterministic μ pathway excluding logvar
task-specific insensitivity
inactive neural units
zero sample gradients
```

Therefore the following are reported:

```text
total Fisher elements
non-zero Fisher elements
zero Fisher elements
non-zero fraction
```


==================================================
## 27. FISHER SCALE DIAGNOSTICS
==================================================

For both encoder and predictor Fisher tensors, Phase 13 reports:

```text
minimum
maximum
mean
median
standard deviation
sum
non-zero elements
zero elements
non-zero fraction
```

Statistics are reported separately for:

\[
F_E
\]

and:

\[
F_P
\]


==================================================
## 28. NORMALIZED IMPORTANCE
==================================================

Raw Fisher values remain the primary quantities preserved for future EWC.

For reporting and comparison only, optional normalized importance is calculated as:

\[
F_{\text{normalized},j}
=
\frac{
F_j
}{
\sum_k F_k+\epsilon
}
\]

The normalized values are used only to interpret relative importance.

They do not overwrite the raw Fisher tensors.


==================================================
## 29. BASELINE PARAMETER REFERENCE
==================================================

Future EWC requires both:

\[
\theta_j^*
\]

and:

\[
F_j
\]

for each EWC-controlled parameter.

Therefore Phase 13 stores:

```text
encoder θE*
encoder F_E

predictor θP*
predictor F_P
```

The decoder:

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

remains part of the complete baseline model state but does not receive a Fisher tensor in the current implementation.


==================================================
## 30. BASELINE INTEGRITY VERIFICATION
==================================================

Before Fisher estimation, Phase 13 verifies that the current encoder, decoder, and predictor checkpoint state dictionaries exactly match the Phase-12:

\[
\Theta^*
\]

reference bundle.

Specifically:

```text
current θE* == Phase-12 θE*
current θD* == Phase-12 θD*
current θP* == Phase-12 θP*
```

This parameter-level verification ensures Fisher is being calculated from the correct baseline model.


==================================================
## 31. SHA-256 CHECKPOINT INTEGRITY
==================================================

Before Fisher estimation, SHA-256 hashes are calculated for:

```text
Phase-10 encoder checkpoint
Phase-11 decoder checkpoint
Phase-12 predictor checkpoint
```

After Fisher estimation, the hashes are calculated again.

Required result:

\[
hash_{\text{before}}
=
hash_{\text{after}}
\]

for every baseline checkpoint.

This verifies that Fisher estimation did not overwrite or alter the saved baseline model files.


==================================================
## 32. FISHER REFERENCE TRACEABILITY
==================================================

Phase 13 saves an explicit Fisher-reference manifest.

For every Fisher molecule the manifest records:

```text
graph_id
drug_id
resolved graph file
number of selected target labels
whether at least one selected target is present
```

This makes the Fisher calculation auditable and reproducible.


==================================================
## 33. MOLECULES WITH ZERO SELECTED POSITIVE TARGETS
==================================================

Some Fisher-reference molecules do not contain a positive association among the frozen 130 target classes.

These molecules are retained.

Their target vectors still contain valid negative-label information.

Observed Fisher-reference composition:

```text
Total Fisher molecules                  = 128
With ≥1 selected target                 = 100
With 0 selected targets                 = 28
```

Therefore all 128 molecules contribute to the defined multi-label Fisher objective.


==================================================
## 34. OBSERVED FISHER TASK LOSS
==================================================

The observed Fisher-reference BCE losses were:

```text
Mean Fisher task loss   = 0.16348652
Median Fisher task loss = 0.12749443
```

These values summarize the frozen predictor task loss across the fixed Fisher-reference molecules.

They are not optimization losses because no parameter update occurs.


==================================================
## 35. OBSERVED ENCODER FISHER RESULTS
==================================================

The encoder contains:

```text
70,274 parameter elements
```

Observed encoder Fisher statistics:

```text
Total parameter elements     = 70,274
Non-zero Fisher elements     = 62,945
Zero Fisher elements         = 7,329
Non-zero fraction            = 89.5708%

Minimum Fisher               = 0.0000000000e+00
Maximum Fisher               = 3.3112639189e-01
Mean Fisher                  = 3.2665659091e-04
Median Fisher                = 2.8831998407e-06
Fisher sum                   = 2.2955465317e+01
```

Therefore approximately:

\[
89.57\%
\]

of encoder parameter elements received non-zero importance under the baseline target-association Fisher objective.


==================================================
## 36. OBSERVED PREDICTOR FISHER RESULTS
==================================================

The predictor contains:

```text
8,674 parameter elements
```

Observed predictor Fisher statistics:

```text
Total parameter elements     = 8,674
Non-zero Fisher elements     = 8,674
Zero Fisher elements         = 0
Non-zero fraction            = 100%

Minimum Fisher               = 4.5052281905e-09
Maximum Fisher               = 2.3111002520e-03
Mean Fisher                  = 9.3684247986e-05
Median Fisher                = 3.9271002606e-05
Fisher sum                   = 8.1261718273e-01
```

Thus all predictor parameter elements received non-zero Fisher importance under the defined task.


==================================================
## 37. OBSERVED HIGH-IMPORTANCE PARAMETER GROUPS
==================================================

The strongest Fisher contributions were concentrated in parameter groups involved in constructing and transforming the deterministic latent molecular representation.

Important parameter groups included:

```text
node_embedding.0.weight
mu_head.weight
node_embedding.0.bias
graph_mlp.0.weight
egnn_layers.1.node_norm.bias
graph_mlp.0.bias
egnn_layers.1.node_mlp
egnn_layers.0.node_norm
predictor network layers
```

The particularly strong importance of:

```text
mu_head
node_embedding
graph-level latent transformation
```

is consistent with the Fisher objective because these parameters directly affect:

\[
\mu
\]

which is then used by the target-association predictor.


==================================================
## 38. INTERPRETATION OF FISHER SCALE
==================================================

Absolute Fisher magnitudes should not be interpreted as direct chemical quantities.

For example:

```text
larger encoder Fisher
```

does not mean:

```text
greater chemical activity
greater binding affinity
greater therapeutic relevance
```

Instead, it means:

**the baseline target-association loss is more sensitive to changes in that model parameter under the fixed Fisher-reference dataset.**


==================================================
## 39. CONSOLIDATED KNOWLEDGE STATE
==================================================

After Phase 13, define:

\[
K_0
\]

as the consolidated baseline knowledge state.

For the implemented system:

\[
K_0
=
\{
\Theta^*,
F_E,
F_P,
Z_0
\}
\]

where:

\[
\Theta^*
=
\{
\theta_E^*,
\theta_D^*,
\theta_P^*
\}
\]

Therefore:

\[
K_0
=
\{
\theta_E^*,
\theta_D^*,
\theta_P^*,
F_E,
F_P,
Z_0
\}
\]

The decoder parameter state remains preserved even though:

\[
F_D
\]

is not calculated.


==================================================
## 40. FUTURE EWC OBJECTIVE
==================================================

Phase 13 does **not** apply EWC.

It only prepares the information required for later EWC-controlled adaptation.

During a later adaptation phase, an EWC term may take the form:

\[
\mathcal{L}_{EWC}
=
\lambda_{EWC}
\sum_j
F_j
(\theta_j-\theta_j^*)^2
\]

and the total future adaptation loss may be:

\[
\mathcal{L}_{total}
=
\mathcal{L}_{adapt}
+
\lambda_{EWC}
\sum_j
F_j
(\theta_j-\theta_j^*)^2
\]

where:

\[
\theta_j^*
\]

is the Phase-12 baseline parameter value,

\[
F_j
\]

is the Phase-13 Fisher importance,

\[
\theta_j
\]

is the parameter value during future adaptation,

and:

\[
\lambda_{EWC}
\]

controls the strength of baseline-knowledge preservation.


==================================================
## 41. IMPORTANT INTERPRETATION
==================================================

Fisher importance does **not** represent:

```text
atomic importance
molecular substructure importance
chemical causality
biological causality
binding affinity
clinical efficacy
therapeutic superiority
```

It represents:

**model-parameter importance under the defined baseline task and Fisher-reference corpus.**

Similarly:

\[
F_j=0
\]

does not establish that a parameter is universally useless.

It means that the parameter received no importance signal under this particular Fisher objective.


==================================================
## 42. PHASE-13 SAVED OUTPUTS
==================================================

Phase 13 saves:

```text
phase13_fisher_config.json

phase13_fisher_reference_manifest.csv

phase13_encoder_fisher.pt

phase13_predictor_fisher.pt

phase13_fisher_parameter_reference.pt

phase13_fisher_parameter_statistics.csv

phase13_fisher_layer_statistics.csv

phase13_fisher_top_parameters.csv

phase13_consolidated_knowledge_manifest.json

phase13_qc_summary.csv

phase13_qc_summary.json
```


### Encoder Fisher

```text
phase13_encoder_fisher.pt
```

contains:

\[
F_E
\]


### Predictor Fisher

```text
phase13_predictor_fisher.pt
```

contains:

\[
F_P
\]


### EWC Reference

```text
phase13_fisher_parameter_reference.pt
```

contains baseline parameter values together with their corresponding Fisher importance values.

==================================================

The following conditions were verified:

```text
Fisher reference size = 128                           PASS

No validation molecules used                         PASS

No test molecules used                               PASS

# PHASE 14 — LATENT-SPACE CANDIDATE GENERATION AND PROPOSAL POOL CONSTRUCTION

## OBJECTIVE

Phase 14 begins the first closed-loop discovery cycle.

The purpose of this phase is to generate genuinely new molecular proposals from the learned latent molecular representation rather than simply selecting existing DrugBank molecules as candidate placeholders.

The baseline state available before candidate generation is:

\[
K_0
=
\{
\Theta^*,
F_E,
F_P,
Z_0
\}
\]

where:

\[
\Theta^*
=
\{
\theta_E^*,
\theta_D^*,
\theta_P^*
\}
\]

and:

- \(\theta_E^*\) is the frozen baseline molecular encoder.
- \(\theta_D^*\) is the trained latent-conditioned molecular decoder.
- \(\theta_P^*\) is the baseline DrugBank-grounded target-association predictor.
- \(F_E\) and \(F_P\) are the Phase-13 Fisher importance references.
- \(Z_0\) is the baseline latent molecular representation.

Phase 14 uses the learned latent space and the trained decoder to construct a molecular candidate pool.

The main output is:

\[
C_t
=
\{
c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_n
\}
\]

for closed-loop cycle \(t\).

For the first cycle:

\[
t=1
\]


==================================================
## IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
==================================================

Candidate generation must be distinguished from candidate evaluation.

Phase 14 performs:

```text
latent proposal generation
latent perturbation
latent interpolation
latent neighborhood exploration
decoder-based molecular generation
SELFIES decoding
chemical validation
standardization
deduplication
baseline-relative novelty checking
candidate provenance recording
candidate-pool construction
```

Phase 14 does not yet perform:

```text
EWC parameter updates
encoder adaptation
predictor adaptation
Fisher recalculation
therapeutic optimization
binding-affinity prediction
clinical ranking
parameter drift
```

Candidate scoring and prioritization may occur in the next evaluation stage.


==================================================
## 1. WHY EXISTING DRUGBANK MOLECULES SHOULD NOT BE THE FINAL CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

Existing DrugBank molecules may be useful during early debugging because they provide known valid molecular structures.

However, using existing DrugBank molecules as the final candidate pool would not demonstrate generative exploration.

The final implementation should therefore demonstrate:

\[
\text{learned latent representation}
\rightarrow
\text{new latent proposal}
\rightarrow
\theta_D^*
\rightarrow
\text{new molecular candidate}
\]

wherever computationally feasible.

DrugBank molecules remain useful as:

```text
latent seed molecules
reference molecules
novelty comparison corpus
similarity anchors
baseline controls
```

but they should not simply be relabeled as newly generated candidates.


==================================================
## 2. CANDIDATE GENERATION SOURCES
==================================================

Candidates may originate from several complementary proposal mechanisms.

Recommended mechanisms are:

### A. Latent Perturbation

For baseline latent vector:

\[
z_i
\]

generate:

\[
z_i'
=
z_i
+
\epsilon
\]

where:

\[
\epsilon
\sim
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)
\]

Small perturbations explore the local neighborhood around a known molecular representation.


### B. Neighborhood Sampling

Generate multiple local samples around selected seed latents:

\[
z_{i,k}
=
z_i
+
\epsilon_k
\]

for:

\[
k=1,\ldots,m
\]

This provides a local molecular neighborhood for each selected seed.


### C. Latent Interpolation

For two baseline latent vectors:

\[
z_a
\]

and:

\[
z_b
\]

construct:

\[
z(\alpha)
=
(1-\alpha)z_a
+
\alpha z_b
\]

with:

\[
0 < \alpha < 1
\]

Interpolation explores molecular representations between known regions of latent space.


### D. Prior / Latent Sampling

Samples may also be generated from a latent prior such as:

\[
z
\sim
\mathcal{N}(0,I)
\]

This is more exploratory than local perturbation.

Because the learned latent distribution may not perfectly match the theoretical prior, prior samples should be treated as exploratory proposals rather than automatically assumed to occupy chemically reliable latent regions.


### E. Decoder-Driven Stochastic Generation

For a fixed latent vector:

\[
z
\]

the decoder may generate multiple molecular sequences using stochastic token sampling.

Thus:

\[
z
\rightarrow
\theta_D^*
\rightarrow
c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_m
\]

The same latent region may therefore yield several different molecular proposals.


==================================================
## 3. RECOMMENDED FIRST-CYCLE GENERATION STRATEGY
==================================================

For the first closed-loop cycle, the most defensible candidate proposal strategy is a mixture of:

```text
local latent perturbation
+
latent interpolation
+
limited exploratory prior sampling
+
stochastic decoder sampling
```

This gives a balance between:

```text
exploitation of known chemical regions
and
exploration of new latent regions
```


==================================================
## 4. BASELINE LATENT SEEDS
==================================================

Candidate generation should begin from selected latent vectors in:

\[
Z_0
\]

Seed molecules should come only from the baseline corpus.

For each seed record:

```text
graph_id
drug_id
baseline latent vector
generation method
generation parameters
```

Seed selection should be deterministic and reproducible.

A fixed random seed should be used where random sampling is required.


==================================================
## 5. LOCAL LATENT PERTURBATION
==================================================

For each selected baseline seed:

\[
z_{\text{seed}}
\]

generate multiple perturbed vectors:

\[
z'
=
z_{\text{seed}}
+
\sigma\epsilon
\]

where:

\[
\epsilon
\sim
\mathcal{N}(0,I)
\]

The perturbation magnitude:

\[
\sigma
\]

must be explicitly recorded.

Because Phase 11 showed that larger perturbations produced larger molecular changes than smaller perturbations, Phase 14 should avoid arbitrarily large latent steps.

A practical initial perturbation schedule may contain several controlled values such as:

```text
small perturbation
moderate perturbation
exploratory perturbation
```

These should be treated as implementation parameters rather than universal scientific constants.


==================================================
## 6. LATENT INTERPOLATION
==================================================

Selected pairs of baseline latent vectors may be interpolated.

For seed pair:

\[
(z_a,z_b)
\]

generate:

\[
z_\alpha
=
(1-\alpha)z_a+\alpha z_b
\]

for selected interpolation coefficients.

Example:

\[
\alpha
\in
\{
0.25,
0.50,
0.75
\}
\]

Interpolation provenance must record:

```text
source drug A
source drug B
alpha
interpolated latent vector
```


==================================================
## 7. PRIOR SAMPLING
==================================================

Exploratory latent samples may be drawn from:

\[
\mathcal{N}(0,I)
\]

However, these samples should form only part of the candidate pool.

They should not dominate the first cycle because the learned latent manifold may differ from an ideal standard normal prior.

Prior-generated candidates should therefore be tagged as:

```text
exploratory_prior
```


==================================================
## 8. DECODER GENERATION
==================================================

Every proposed latent vector is passed through the frozen Phase-11 molecular decoder:

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

The decoder should remain unchanged in Phase 14.

The generation process is:

```text
candidate latent vector
        ↓
frozen θD*
        ↓
SELFIES token generation
        ↓
SELFIES sequence
        ↓
SMILES
        ↓
molecular candidate
```

Generation may use:

```text
temperature-controlled sampling
top-k sampling
greedy decoding for diagnostics
```

The exact generation parameters must be recorded.


==================================================
## 9. MULTIPLE MOLECULES PER LATENT
==================================================

A latent vector does not have to produce only one candidate.

For each proposed latent vector:

\[
z_i'
\]

the decoder may generate multiple stochastic sequences:

\[
c_{i,1},
c_{i,2},
\ldots,
c_{i,m}
\]

This allows molecular diversity to emerge even within a single latent neighborhood.


==================================================
## 10. SELFIES DECODING
==================================================

Generated decoder output should first be interpreted as a SELFIES sequence.

The candidate sequence must successfully convert:

\[
\text{SELFIES}
\rightarrow
\text{SMILES}
\]

Candidates that fail SELFIES decoding should be rejected and recorded as:

```text
selfies_decode_failure
```


==================================================
## 11. RDKIT PARSING
==================================================

Decoded SMILES should be parsed with RDKit.

Recommended sequence:

```text
SMILES
↓
MolFromSmiles(..., sanitize=False)
↓
SanitizeMol
```

Candidates that fail parsing or sanitization must be excluded from the valid candidate set.


==================================================
## 12. CHEMICAL STANDARDIZATION
==================================================

Successfully parsed candidates should be standardized using the same chemical-standardization principles established earlier.

Recommended steps include:

```text
RDKit Cleanup
FragmentParent
Uncharger
final sanitization
canonical SMILES
```

The standardized canonical SMILES should represent the final candidate identity used for deduplication.


==================================================
## 13. VALENCE VALIDATION
==================================================

Generated molecules should pass explicit valence/property-cache checks.

Candidates with invalid atomic valence or sanitization errors must not enter the final candidate pool.


==================================================
## 14. MODEL-FEASIBILITY HEAVY-ATOM FILTER
==================================================

Apply the existing model-feasibility range:

\[
4
\le
\text{heavy atoms}
\le
80
\]

This should continue to be described as:

**model feasibility filtering**

and not as a universal chemical-validity rule.


==================================================
## 15. DUPLICATE REMOVAL
==================================================

After canonicalization, duplicate molecules must be removed.

Two generated candidates with the same canonical standardized SMILES represent the same molecular candidate.

Therefore retain one candidate identity while preserving generation provenance where useful.


==================================================
## 16. BASELINE-RELATIVE NOVELTY
==================================================

Novelty should be defined relative to the standardized baseline DrugBank molecular corpus.

For generated candidate:

\[
c
\]

define:

```text
novel = True
```

when its canonical standardized SMILES is absent from the baseline corpus.

This should be described explicitly as:

**novel relative to the baseline DrugBank molecular corpus**

and not as globally novel chemistry.


==================================================
## 17. GENERATED-CANDIDATE PROVENANCE
==================================================

Every candidate should preserve its origin.

Recommended provenance fields include:

```text
candidate_id
cycle
generation_method
seed_graph_id
seed_drug_id
second_seed_graph_id if interpolation
second_seed_drug_id if interpolation
interpolation_alpha
perturbation_sigma
latent_sample_index
decoder_sample_index
temperature
top_k
generated_SELFIES
decoded_SMILES
canonical_SMILES
validity_status
novel_vs_baseline
```

This is particularly important for patent and thesis reproducibility.


==================================================
## 18. CANDIDATE IDENTIFIER
==================================================

Assign each unique validated candidate a stable identifier.

For example:

```text
CYCLE01_CAND000001
CYCLE01_CAND000002
...
```

This identifier should be used consistently throughout later:

```text
evaluation
ranking
selection
feedback
adaptation
drift analysis
```


==================================================
## 19. RAW CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

Let:

\[
C_t^{raw}
\]

represent all decoder outputs before chemical QC.

This includes:

```text
valid candidates
invalid SELFIES
invalid SMILES
sanitization failures
heavy-atom failures
duplicates
baseline molecules
```


==================================================
## 20. VALIDATED CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

After SELFIES decoding, parsing, sanitization, standardization, and model-feasibility checks:

\[
C_t^{valid}
\]

contains chemically processable candidates under the defined computational QC pipeline.


==================================================
## 21. UNIQUE CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

After canonical deduplication:

\[
C_t^{unique}
\]

contains unique validated molecular candidates.


==================================================
## 22. NOVEL CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

After comparison against the baseline DrugBank corpus:

\[
C_t^{novel}
\]

contains unique candidates absent from the baseline molecular corpus.

Therefore:

\[
C_t^{novel}
\subseteq
C_t^{unique}
\subseteq
C_t^{valid}
\subseteq
C_t^{raw}
\]


==================================================
## 23. FINAL PHASE-14 CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

The final candidate pool used by the next evaluation stage should preferably be:

\[
C_t
=
C_t^{novel}
\]

or a documented subset of \(C_t^{novel}\) if a maximum pool size is required.

Thus:

\[
C_t
=
\{
c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_n
\}
\]

represents unique, validated, baseline-relative novel molecular proposals generated from the learned latent representation.


==================================================
## 24. GENERATION-DIVERSITY DIAGNOSTICS
==================================================

Phase 14 should report:

```text
number of raw generated sequences
SELFIES decode success rate
RDKit parse success rate
sanitization success rate
standardization success rate
model-feasibility pass rate
chemical validity rate
number of unique candidates
uniqueness rate
number novel vs baseline
novelty rate
mean fingerprint diversity
```

These metrics should be reported separately for each generation strategy where practical.


==================================================
## 25. GENERATION METHOD COMPARISON
==================================================

Recommended method-level reporting:

```text
latent perturbation
latent interpolation
prior sampling
decoder stochastic resampling
```

For each method record:

```text
attempted
valid
unique
novel
validity %
uniqueness %
novelty %
diversity
```

This allows later analysis of which proposal mechanism contributes useful candidate diversity.


==================================================
## 26. LATENT-DISTANCE RECORDING
==================================================

For perturbation-generated candidates record:

\[
\|z'-z_{\text{seed}}\|_2
\]

For interpolation-generated candidates record distances to both source latents.

For prior-generated candidates, optionally record distance to the nearest baseline latent representation.

These values can later help investigate whether candidate quality deteriorates far from the baseline latent manifold.


==================================================
## 27. OPTIONAL NEAREST-BASELINE SIMILARITY
==================================================

For each generated candidate, molecular fingerprint similarity to the nearest baseline molecule may be calculated.

This can help distinguish:

```text
close analogues
moderately novel structures
highly dissimilar proposals
```

However, similarity should not be interpreted as biological activity.


==================================================
## 28. IMPORTANT ROLE OF PHASE-11 VALIDATION
==================================================

Phase 11 already demonstrated that the decoder responds measurably to changes in the latent representation.

Therefore Phase 14 is not simply generating arbitrary molecular strings.

It explicitly exploits the learned mapping:

\[
z
\rightarrow
\theta_D^*
\rightarrow
\text{molecular sequence}
\]

to explore molecular neighborhoods and new latent locations.


==================================================
## 29. DECODER REMAINS FROZEN
==================================================

During Phase 14:

\[
\theta_D
=
\theta_D^*
\]

The decoder generates candidates but is not trained or updated.

Likewise, candidate generation itself must not alter:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

or:

\[
\theta_P^*
\]


==================================================
## 30. NO EWC YET DURING GENERATION
==================================================

The Fisher information produced in Phase 13 is preserved for later adaptation.

Phase 14 candidate generation alone does not require an EWC penalty because no trainable parameter update occurs.

Thus:

```text
F_E = unchanged
F_P = unchanged
Θ* = unchanged
K0 = preserved
```


==================================================
## 31. CANDIDATE GENERATION IS NOT CANDIDATE SELECTION
==================================================

Generation should produce a sufficiently diverse candidate set before biological relevance or acquisition criteria are applied.

Therefore Phase 14 should not silently remove molecules simply because their current predictor score is low.

Otherwise proposal generation and evaluation become mixed together.

Recommended separation:

```text
Phase 14
Generate molecular possibilities

Phase 15
Evaluate / score / prioritize molecular possibilities
```


==================================================
## 32. CANDIDATE POOL SIZE
==================================================

Define a reproducible proposal budget.

For example:

```text
N_seed
N_perturbations_per_seed
N_interpolation_pairs
N_interpolation_points
N_prior_latents
N_decoder_samples_per_latent
```

The exact numbers are implementation choices and should be explicitly saved in the Phase-14 configuration.

Candidate pool size should be reported both:

```text
before QC
and
after QC
```


==================================================
## 33. RANDOMNESS AND REPRODUCIBILITY
==================================================

All random operations should use a fixed seed.

This includes:

```text
seed molecule selection
latent perturbation
latent pair selection
prior sampling
decoder token sampling
```

The seed must be saved in Phase-14 metadata.


==================================================
## 34. RECOMMENDED GENERATION POLICY FOR CYCLE 1
==================================================

A practical first-cycle proposal policy is:

```text
Baseline latent seeds Z0
        ↓
Local perturbation candidates
+
Interpolation candidates
+
Limited prior candidates
        ↓
Frozen Phase-11 decoder
        ↓
Multiple stochastic molecular proposals
        ↓
Chemical QC
        ↓
Deduplication
        ↓
Baseline-relative novelty
        ↓
C1
```


==================================================

==================================================

Recommended candidate table fields:

```text

## 37. PHASE-14 QUALITY CONTROL
==================================================

Verify:

```text
Phase-12 decoder checkpoint loads

decoder state equals θD*

```


==================================================
## 38. PHASE-14 COMPLETION CRITERIA
==================================================

Phase 14 is complete when:

1. The frozen baseline state is loaded.

2. The Phase-11 molecular decoder matches \(\theta_D^*\).

3. \(Z_0\) is loaded.

4. Latent dimensionality remains 32.

5. Seed latent vectors are selected reproducibly.

6. Local latent perturbation proposals are created.

7. Interpolation proposals are created.

8. Limited exploratory latent-prior samples are created.

9. All proposed latent vectors are finite.

10. Proposed latents are passed through the frozen generative decoder.

11. Molecular SELFIES sequences are produced.

12. SELFIES-to-SMILES decoding is performed.

13. RDKit parsing is performed.

14. Sanitization is performed.

15. Standardization is performed.

16. Valence checks are performed.

17. Model-feasibility filtering is performed.

18. Valid candidates are identified.

19. Canonical duplicates are removed.

20. Novelty against the baseline DrugBank corpus is calculated.

21. Candidate provenance is retained.

22. Generation-method statistics are calculated.

23. Candidate diversity is calculated.

24. A final unique validated candidate pool is produced.

25. A baseline-relative novel candidate pool is produced.

26. \(\theta_E^*\) remains unchanged.

27. \(\theta_D^*\) remains unchanged.

28. \(\theta_P^*\) remains unchanged.

29. No EWC occurs.

30. No parameter adaptation occurs.


==================================================
## 39. SCIENTIFIC INTERPRETATION
==================================================

After successful Phase 14 it is appropriate to state:

> “Molecular candidates were generated from the learned molecular latent representation using local perturbation, latent interpolation, exploratory prior sampling, and stochastic decoding.”

It is also appropriate to state:

> “Generated candidates were subjected to SELFIES decoding, RDKit parsing, sanitization, standardization, model-feasibility filtering, canonical deduplication, and baseline-relative novelty assessment.”

It is also appropriate to state:

> “The resulting candidate pool contains computational molecular proposals generated by the frozen baseline molecular decoder.”


==================================================
## 40. CLAIMS THAT SHOULD NOT YET BE MADE
==================================================

Do not yet claim:

```text
generated molecules are active drugs

generated molecules bind a particular target

generated molecules have improved affinity

generated molecules are therapeutically superior

generated molecules are safe

generated molecules are synthesizable

candidate generation improved the model

EWC prevented forgetting

the model has self-evolved
```

Those require later evaluation and adaptation stages.

## NEXT PHASE
-------------
==================
# PHASE 15 — CHEMICAL ELIGIBILITY AND PRE-EVALUATION SCREENING


## OBJECTIVE

Phase 15 performs a formal chemical eligibility and pre-evaluation screening of the molecular candidates generated during Phase 14.

The Phase-14 candidate hierarchy is:

\[
C_1^{raw}
\supseteq
C_1^{valid}
\supseteq
C_1^{unique}
\supseteq
C_1^{novel}
\]

The principal input to Phase 15 is:

\[
C_1^{novel}
\]

which contains unique, chemically valid, baseline-relative novel molecular proposals generated from the learned latent representation.

Phase 15 determines which of these molecules are sufficiently well-formed and physicochemically characterized to enter the later in-silico biological evaluation engine.

The principal Phase-15 output is:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
\]

where:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
\subseteq
C_1^{novel}
\]

Candidates failing strict structural or numerical eligibility requirements are placed in:

\[
C_1^{ineligible}
\]


==================================================
## IMPORTANT PHASE BOUNDARY
==================================================

Phase 15 performs:

```text
chemical eligibility screening
structural integrity verification
fragment checking
molecular-size verification
physicochemical descriptor calculation
descriptor finiteness checking
soft drug-likeness characterization
candidate eligibility classification
audit logging
```

Phase 15 does **not** perform:

```text
biological target-association scoring
binding-affinity prediction
therapeutic efficacy prediction
candidate utility ranking
UCB acquisition
EWC
model parameter updates
closed-loop adaptation
```

Therefore:

\[
\text{chemical eligibility}
\neq
\text{biological efficacy}
\]


==================================================
## 1. INPUT CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

Load the finalized Phase-14 novel candidate pool:

\[
C_1^{novel}
\]

Candidate identifiers and canonical molecular representations established in Phase 14 must be preserved.

Phase 15 should not generate new molecules.

It only evaluates the eligibility of existing Phase-14 candidates.


==================================================
## 2. PRESERVE PHASE-14 MOLECULAR IDENTITY
==================================================

The Phase-14 standardized canonical SMILES should remain the authoritative candidate identity.

Phase 15 should:

```text
load canonical SMILES
↓
reparse with RDKit
↓
verify chemical integrity
↓
calculate descriptors
```

Phase 15 should not silently perform a new independent standardization procedure that changes candidate identity.

This ensures that:

\[
candidate\_id
\leftrightarrow
canonical\_smiles
\]

remains stable across pipeline phases.


==================================================
## 3. CANDIDATE HIERARCHY
==================================================

The complete candidate hierarchy becomes:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
\subseteq
C_1^{novel}
\subseteq
C_1^{unique}
\subseteq
C_1^{valid}
\subseteq
C_1^{raw}
\]

This ensures that only genuinely generated, unique, baseline-relative novel candidates proceed into downstream evaluation.


==================================================
## 4. WHY PHASE 15 IS REQUIRED
==================================================

A molecule may be syntactically valid but still be unsuitable for downstream computational evaluation.

For example, a candidate may have:

```text
unusual molecular size
extreme lipophilicity
extreme polarity
large formal charge
excessive flexibility
disconnected fragments
non-finite descriptor values
```

Therefore:

\[
valid
\neq
evaluation-ready
\]

Phase 15 provides an explicit eligibility gate before biological scoring.


==================================================
## 5. STRUCTURAL VALIDITY RECONFIRMATION
==================================================

For every Phase-14 novel candidate, reconfirm:

```text
canonical SMILES present
RDKit parsing successful
RDKit sanitization successful
property-cache update successful
valence representation valid
molecule contains atoms
```

These checks verify that no malformed candidate enters later evaluation.


==================================================
## 6. UNIQUENESS RECONFIRMATION
==================================================

Verify that standardized canonical SMILES remain unique.

For candidates:

\[
c_i
\]

and:

\[
c_j
\]

require:

\[
SMILES_{canonical}(c_i)
\neq
SMILES_{canonical}(c_j)
\]

for:

\[
i\neq j
\]

Duplicate identities should not be evaluated as separate candidates.


==================================================
## 7. BASELINE-RELATIVE NOVELTY RECONFIRMATION
==================================================

Retain the Phase-14 novelty definition.

Candidate:

\[
c_i
\]

is considered novel when its standardized canonical SMILES is absent from the baseline DrugBank molecular corpus.

Thus:

\[
c_i
\notin
D_{baseline}
\]

The terminology must remain:

**novel relative to the baseline DrugBank corpus**

and not:

**globally novel molecule**.


==================================================
## 8. HARD ELIGIBILITY RULES
==================================================

A candidate should be classified as chemically ineligible only for strict structural or numerical failure modes.

Recommended hard rejection conditions are:

```text
RDKit parse failure

sanitization failure

property-cache / valence failure

empty molecular structure

missing canonical SMILES

disconnected fragments remaining after Phase-14 standardization

non-finite required descriptor values

heavy atom count outside 4–80
```

These are eligibility failures rather than biological judgments.


==================================================
## 9. DISCONNECTED FRAGMENT CHECK
==================================================

For each candidate calculate:

\[
N_{fragments}
\]

using the authoritative Phase-14 canonical molecular representation.

Require:

\[
N_{fragments}=1
\]

for chemical eligibility.

If:

\[
N_{fragments}>1
\]

the candidate should be excluded and recorded as:

```text
disconnected_fragments
```

Because Phase 14 used fragment-parent standardization, such cases should normally be uncommon.


==================================================
## 10. MODEL-FEASIBILITY HEAVY-ATOM RANGE
==================================================

Retain the previously established model-feasibility requirement:

\[
4
\le
N_{heavy}
\le
80
\]

Candidates outside this interval are excluded from downstream evaluation.

This remains a:

**MODEL-FEASIBILITY CONSTRAINT**

and must not be presented as a universal definition of chemical validity.


==================================================
## 11. PHYSICOCHEMICAL DESCRIPTOR SET
==================================================

For each candidate calculate the following core descriptors:

```text
molecular weight
heavy atom count
cLogP
topological polar surface area
hydrogen-bond donors
hydrogen-bond acceptors
rotatable bonds
formal charge
ring count
aromatic ring count
fraction Csp3
```

These descriptors provide a standardized chemical profile for subsequent candidate evaluation.


==================================================
## 12. MOLECULAR WEIGHT
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
MW(c_i)
\]

using molecular weight in:

\[
g/mol
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
RDKit Descriptors.MolWt
```

Molecular weight is stored as a continuous descriptor.

It is not by itself a hard rejection criterion unless explicitly required by a later methodology.


==================================================
## 13. HEAVY ATOM COUNT
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
N_{heavy}
\]

using:

```text
Mol.GetNumHeavyAtoms()
```

This descriptor is also used for the established model-feasibility constraint:

\[
4
\le
N_{heavy}
\le
80
\]


==================================================
## 14. cLogP
==================================================

Calculate molecular lipophilicity using Wildman-Crippen LogP:

\[
cLogP(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Crippen.MolLogP
```

cLogP is retained as a continuous descriptor.

Extreme values may be flagged but should not automatically invalidate an otherwise structurally sound molecule.


==================================================
## 15. TOPOLOGICAL POLAR SURFACE AREA
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
TPSA(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
rdMolDescriptors.CalcTPSA
```

TPSA characterizes molecular polarity.

It is used as a physicochemical descriptor rather than evidence of biological activity.


==================================================
## 16. HYDROGEN-BOND DONORS
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
HBD(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Lipinski.NumHDonors
```

or the corresponding RDKit hydrogen-bond donor function available in the environment.


==================================================
## 17. HYDROGEN-BOND ACCEPTORS
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
HBA(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Lipinski.NumHAcceptors
```

or the corresponding RDKit hydrogen-bond acceptor function available in the environment.


==================================================
## 18. ROTATABLE BONDS
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
N_{rot}(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Lipinski.NumRotatableBonds
```

This provides a measure of molecular flexibility.


==================================================
## 19. FORMAL CHARGE
==================================================

Calculate total molecular formal charge:

\[
Q_{formal}(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Chem.GetFormalCharge
```

Large absolute charge values may generate a soft physicochemical flag.

They should not automatically imply biological failure.


==================================================
## 20. RING COUNT
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
N_{rings}(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Lipinski.RingCount
```

This provides a basic measure of molecular cyclic complexity.


==================================================
## 21. AROMATIC RING COUNT
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
N_{aromatic}(c_i)
\]

using the corresponding RDKit aromatic-ring descriptor.

This provides additional structural characterization.


==================================================
## 22. FRACTION CSP3
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
F_{sp3}(c_i)
\]

Recommended implementation:

```text
Lipinski.FractionCSP3
```

Fraction Csp3 characterizes molecular saturation and three-dimensional carbon character.

It is descriptive and should not be interpreted directly as therapeutic quality.


==================================================
## 23. DESCRIPTOR FINITENESS
==================================================

All required descriptor values must be finite.

Require:

```text
no NaN

no +infinity

no -infinity
```

Formally:

\[
descriptor(c_i)
\in
\mathbb{R}
\]

for every required descriptor.

A candidate with a non-finite critical descriptor is excluded from:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
\]


==================================================
## 24. LIPINSKI RULE-OF-FIVE CHARACTERIZATION
==================================================

Calculate a conventional Lipinski Rule-of-Five violation count using:

\[
MW>500
\]

\[
cLogP>5
\]

\[
HBD>5
\]

\[
HBA>10
\]

For every candidate define:

\[
N_{LipinskiViolations}
\]

as the number of violated conditions.

Recommended fields:

```text
lipinski_violation_count

lipinski_soft_flag
```

The soft flag may be defined as:

```text
lipinski_soft_flag = True
if lipinski_violation_count > 1
```

However, Lipinski violations remain:

**SOFT PHYSICOCHEMICAL FLAGS**

They are not hard Phase-15 exclusion criteria.


==================================================
## 25. HARD EXCLUSION VS SOFT FLAGGING
==================================================

Phase 15 explicitly separates:

### HARD ELIGIBILITY FAILURES

```text
invalid canonical representation
RDKit parse failure
sanitization failure
valence failure
disconnected molecular fragments
heavy atoms outside 4–80
non-finite descriptors
```

These prevent entry into:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
\]


### SOFT PHYSICOCHEMICAL FLAGS

```text
high molecular weight
high cLogP
high TPSA
high HBD
high HBA
many rotatable bonds
large absolute formal charge
multiple Lipinski violations
```

Soft flags remain attached to the candidate but do not automatically cause exclusion.


==================================================
## 26. WHY SOFT FLAGS ARE IMPORTANT
==================================================

The molecular generator is intended to explore chemical space.

Overly aggressive rule-based exclusion could remove potentially interesting candidates before biological scoring.

Therefore the preferred strategy is:

\[
strict\ structural\ validity
+
soft\ physicochemical\ characterization
\]

rather than:

\[
broad\ heuristic\ rejection
\]


==================================================
## 27. QED
==================================================

Calculate:

\[
QED(c_i)
\]

for every structurally eligible candidate.

QED may be stored using the standard RDKit QED implementation.

QED is treated as a:

**passive computational molecular descriptor**

during Phase 15.

It may later contribute to candidate prioritization in Phase 16.

However:

\[
QED
\neq
biological\ activity
\]

\[
QED
\neq
therapeutic\ efficacy
\]

\[
QED
\neq
experimental\ validation
\]


==================================================
## 28. SYNTHETIC ACCESSIBILITY SCORE
==================================================

Synthetic accessibility may also be calculated as:

\[
SA(c_i)
\]

if a standard and explicitly identifiable SA-score implementation is available in the computational environment.

The preferred policy is:

```text
if standard SA scorer available:
    calculate SA
    record implementation/source
    store score

otherwise:
    do not invent or substitute an undocumented SA approximation
```

SA is treated as a passive numerical descriptor.

It should not be described as experimental proof that a molecule can or cannot be synthesized.


==================================================
## 29. QED AND SA PLACEMENT
==================================================

QED and SA may be calculated at the end of Phase 15 so that Phase 16 can directly use them during multi-objective candidate prioritization.

Thus Phase 15 may produce:

\[
QED(c_i)
\]

and:

\[
SA(c_i)
\]

without yet combining them into a final candidate score.

Their integration into acquisition or utility scoring belongs to the later evaluation phase.


==================================================
## 30. OPTIONAL STRUCTURAL ALERTS
==================================================

Optional structural-alert screening may include:

```text
PAINS alerts
reactive-substructure alerts
undesirable-substructure alerts
```

If implemented, these should normally be recorded as:

**structural alert flags**

rather than unconditional proof that a candidate is invalid.

The exact alert library and implementation should be documented.


==================================================
## 31. CHEMICAL ELIGIBILITY DEFINITION
==================================================

For candidate:

\[
c_i
\]

define:

\[
E_i
\]

as the hard-exclusion indicator.

If any hard eligibility condition fails:

\[
E_i=1
\]

Otherwise:

\[
E_i=0
\]

Then define:

\[
eligible(c_i)
=
1-E_i
\]

The Phase-15 eligible pool is:

\[
C_1^{eligible}
=
\{
c_i\in C_1^{novel}
:
eligible(c_i)=1
\}
\]


==================================================
## 32. INELIGIBLE CANDIDATE POOL
==================================================

Candidates failing one or more hard eligibility rules are assigned to:

\[
C_1^{ineligible}
\]

Every ineligible molecule must preserve:

```text
candidate_id
canonical_smiles
rejection status
rejection reason
all successfully calculated descriptors
generation provenance
```

No candidate should be silently deleted.


==================================================
## 33. REJECTION REASONS
==================================================

Recommended rejection categories:

```text
missing_canonical_smiles

rdkit_parse_failure

sanitize_failure

valence_failure

empty_molecule

disconnected_fragments

outside_model_feasibility

non_finite_descriptor
```

If multiple failures occur, preserve all relevant failure reasons where practical.


==================================================
## 34. CANDIDATE SCREENING TABLE
==================================================

The comprehensive Phase-15 screening table should contain at minimum:

```


==================================================
## 35. SOFT PHYSICOCHEMICAL FLAG TABLE
==================================================

Optional soft flags may include:

```text
high_mw

high_clogp

high_tpsa

high_hbd

high_hba

high_rotatable_bonds

large_absolute_formal_charge

multiple_lipinski_violations
```

These should be stored for later interpretation.

They should not automatically remove a structurally valid molecule from the candidate pool.


==================================================
## 36. COUNT CONSERVATION
==================================================

An essential Phase-15 QC requirement is:

\[
N_{input}
=
N_{eligible}
+
N_{ineligible}
\]

Therefore:

\[
|C_1^{novel}|
=
|C_1^{eligible}|
+
|C_1^{ineligible}|
\]

Every input candidate must be represented exactly once in the final eligibility classification.

==================================================

Phase 15 performs no model training.

Therefore:

\[
\theta_E^*
\]

remains unchanged.

\[
\theta_D^*
\]

remains unchanged.

\[
\theta_P^*
\]

remains unchanged.

Likewise:

\[
F_E
\]

and:

\[
F_P
\]

remain unchanged.

Therefore the consolidated baseline knowledge state:

\[
K_0
\]

is preserved throughout Phase 15.


==================================================
## 43. NO EWC IN PHASE 15
==================================================

Because no parameter optimization occurs:

```text
optimizer created = False

optimizer step = False

EWC applied = False

model adaptation = False
```

The Fisher information remains stored for later continual-learning adaptation.


==================================================
## 44. NO BIOLOGICAL SCORING IN PHASE 15
==================================================

Phase 15 does not use:

\[
\theta_P^*
\]

to rank candidates biologically.

The baseline target-association predictor remains unchanged.

Biological relevance scoring belongs to Phase 16.

## 46. COMPLETION CRITERIA
==================================================

Phase 15 is complete when:

1. The finalized Phase-14 novel candidate pool is loaded.

2. Candidate IDs are preserved.

3. Canonical molecular identities are preserved.

4. Candidate uniqueness remains valid.

5. Baseline-relative novelty remains valid.

6. RDKit parsing is verified.

7. Sanitization is verified.

8. Property-cache and valence checks are performed.

9. Fragment count is calculated.

10. Single-fragment integrity is verified.

11. Heavy atom count is calculated.

12. Heavy atom feasibility 4–80 is applied.

13. Molecular weight is calculated.

14. cLogP is calculated.

15. TPSA is calculated.

16. Hydrogen-bond donors are calculated.

17. Hydrogen-bond acceptors are calculated.

18. Rotatable bonds are calculated.

19. Formal charge is calculated.

20. Ring count is calculated.

21. Aromatic ring count is calculated.

22. Fraction Csp3 is calculated.

23. Lipinski violation count is calculated.

24. Lipinski soft flag is calculated.

25. QED is calculated.

26. SA is calculated if the standard implementation is available.

27. All required descriptor values are finite.

28. Hard-exclusion rules are applied.

29. Soft physicochemical flags are retained.

30. All rejection reasons are recorded.

31. \(C_1^{eligible}\) is constructed.

32. \(C_1^{ineligible}\) is constructed.

33. Input candidate count is conserved.

34. Descriptor distributions are summarized.

35. Baseline parameter checkpoints remain unchanged.

36. Fisher references remain unchanged.

37. No optimizer update occurs.

38. No EWC occurs.

39. No biological ranking occurs.

40. No closed-loop model adaptation occurs.


==================================================
## 47. APPROPRIATE TERMINOLOGY AFTER PHASE 15
==================================================

It is appropriate to state:

> “Generated molecular candidates were subjected to an auditable chemical eligibility screen based on structural validity, valence correctness, fragment integrity, model-feasibility constraints, descriptor finiteness, and physicochemical characterization.”


It is appropriate to state:

> “Candidates satisfying the predefined hard structural eligibility criteria were retained as the chemically eligible pool for subsequent in-silico biological evaluation.”


It is appropriate to state:

> “Lipinski-style properties, QED, and other physicochemical descriptors were retained as descriptive or soft prioritization features rather than interpreted as evidence of biological efficacy.”


If SA was calculated, it is appropriate to state:

> “A computational synthetic-accessibility score was retained as a heuristic descriptor for subsequent candidate prioritization.”


==================================================
## 48. CLAIMS THAT SHOULD NOT BE MADE
==================================================

Do not state:

```text
“The eligible candidates are active drugs.”

“The eligible candidates bind the biological target.”

“The candidates have improved binding affinity.”

“The candidates are therapeutically effective.”

“The candidates are clinically safe.”

“The SA score proves synthesizability.”

“QED proves pharmacological efficacy.”

“Lipinski compliance proves drug efficacy.”

“The model has improved.”

“EWC prevented forgetting.”

“The system has self-evolved.”
```
